approachQuestion.prompt:
One Required Erasure

Given a binary array `bits`, delete exactly one entry. The remaining entries join together. Return the longest contiguous run of ones obtainable after the deletion. Other zeros may remain. A one-entry array yields zero.

Limits and assumptions:
• 1 ≤ n ≤ 200000; each bits[i] is 0 or 1.
• Exactly one deletion is required, including when the array contains only ones. Return only a length, leaving bits unchanged.

Examples:
1. bits = [1,1,0,1] → 3.
2. bits = [1,1,1] → 2.
3. bits = [0] → 0.

Choose one approach.
constraints: Exactly one deletion is required, including when the array contains only ones. Return only a length, leaving bits unchanged.

options.text: Keep the longest moving segment containing at most one zero. For each repaired segment consider its length minus one, and return the greatest such value.
options.feedback: If the segment contains a zero, deleting it joins its ones. If it has no zero, deleting a one satisfies the mandatory operation.

options.text: Try each deletion, scan the resulting conceptual sequence for the longest ones run, and take the greatest.
options.feedback: It respects exactly one deletion and finds the correct answer, but repeats nearly the same scan for every possible erased position.

options.text: Return the length of the longest segment containing at most one zero without subtracting one.
options.feedback: For [1,1,1] the method returns three, but one entry must be deleted and the answer is two.

options.text: Count all ones and return that count unless all entries are ones, in which case subtract one.
options.feedback: For [1,0,0,1], deleting one zero cannot join the separated ones; the answer is one, not two.

details: Track the number of zeros in a window. Extend right and shrink left until at most one zero remains. Update best using right-left, which is window length minus one. Initialize best to zero.

Exactly one deletion is mandatory. A window containing at most one zero yields a run of window length minus one, even if it contains no zero. Returning the full all-one length would violate that required deletion.

“Keep the longest moving segment containing at most one zero. For each repaired segment consider its length minus one, and return the greatest such value.”: If the segment contains a zero, deleting it joins its ones. If it has no zero, deleting a one satisfies the mandatory operation.

“Count all ones and return that count unless all entries are ones, in which case subtract one.”: For [1,0,0,1], deleting one zero cannot join the separated ones; the answer is one, not two.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only “Account for the mandatory deletion” as specified in the method reveal. Choose the tightest worst-case running-time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Use unit-cost random access and arithmetic on machine words large enough for every index and sum.
Input is read-only and excluded from auxiliary space. The scalar or index-pair output is excluded; no candidate segment is copied.
The implementation is iterative with a constant call stack. No hashing is used; fixed alphabet arrays, when present, are direct indexed.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Forward boundaries and one zero counter track the best length after deletion.
details: Every candidate with at most one zero can produce a run of its length minus one by one deletion. Conversely any resulting run comes from a source interval with at most one zero, or an all-one interval with one deletion accounted for. Each boundary advances at most n times, with only scalar counts and indices.
“O(n²) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Removing left entries only while there are two zeros makes each index enter and leave once, rather than retrying every source interval.
“O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: The method tracks one zero count and boundaries, with no sort or helper array.
“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: The input is not copied and zero positions are not collected; scalar window state suffices.
